  "text": "At the end of Harbor Street stood a clock shop that had not kept accurate time in decades. Its clocks chimed at odd hours, and the painted sign above the door had faded until only the word “Tomorrow” remained. Still, every afternoon, Mara opened the shop and swept the floor.

She had inherited it from her uncle, a quiet man who repaired clocks for people who missed someone. “A stopped clock is only waiting,” he used to say. Mara had never understood what he meant.

One rainy Tuesday, a boy appeared at the door carrying a brass pocket watch. He said it had belonged to his mother, who had gone away before he was old enough to remember her. The watch had stopped at 3:17.

Mara opened its back and found a tiny scrap of paper folded beneath the gears. On it, someone had written: “For when you’re ready to hear the story.”

The boy looked up. “Can you fix it?”

Mara studied the watch. Its spring was worn, and its hands had rusted in place. She could repair the spring, but the rest would take patience. So she invited the boy back the next afternoon.

He returned every day, listening as Mara worked. Between the ticking and the turning gears, she told him what she knew of his mother: that she had laughed loudly, hated goodbyes, and once left a note saying she hoped her son would always find his way home.

At last, the watch began to run. The boy held it to his ear, and its steady beat filled the little shop.

Outside, the sign creaked in the wind. For the first time, Mara thought it looked less like a promise and more like an invitation."
